Description: A Sumerian law collection of Lipit-Ishtar, fifth king of the Dynasty of Isin, the second oldest surviving law code after Ur-Nammu and about a century older than Hammurabi's. Its diorite stele, erected at Nippur, survives only in fragments; most of the text comes from scribal-school tablets from Nippur, and about half the code is preserved. It has the classic shape of prologue, laws introduced by 'if', and epilogue with blessings for a king who honours the stele and curses for one who defaces it, covering property, inheritance, marriage, debt, slaves, and hired oxen.
Interpretations: Scholars agree on the code's date, structure, and position between Ur-Nammu and Hammurabi; reconstruction is incomplete, with about half the text lost and the placement of some fragments uncertain.
BiblicalSignificance: Lipit-Ishtar shows that written, case-by-case law ('if a man...') was already ancient in Mesopotamia long before Moses, and it frames the question the Bible itself answers differently: here law comes from a king appointed by the gods, while in Scripture law comes directly from the Lord. Its parallels in family, debt, and injury law sharpen what is distinctive about Exodus and Deuteronomy.
CurrentLocation: Louvre, Paris (prologue fragment); other tablets in museum collections
DiscoveryLocation: Nippur, Iraq (stele erected there; prologue fragment Louvre AO 5473)
